title: Shared responsibility in the cloud: what Microsoft, Google and AWS don't do for you
content:
Moving to Microsoft 365, Google Workspace or AWS doesn't hand your security to the provider. What the shared responsibility model means in practice, and the jobs that always stay with you.

Print / Save PDFOn this page+Moving to Microsoft 365, Google Workspace or AWS doesn't hand your security to the provider. What the shared responsibility model means in practice, and the jobs that always stay with you.

"It's in the cloud, so Microsoft handles security." I hear some version of this every month, usually from a business owner who has moved email to Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace and files to OneDrive or Google Drive. It's an understandable assumption. It's also the reason a lot of small companies find out, after an incident, that some important job was nobody's.

The cloud providers are very clear about where their job ends. They just say it in documentation most people never read. This post translates it into plain terms and gives you a short list of what stays on your side.

content:

Print / Save PDFOn this page+Public buckets, shared snapshots, open RDP and admin accounts without MFA. A practical checklist for AWS, Azure and Google Cloud, written for Sri Lankan companies without a security team.

Most of the cloud problems I get called in for were not clever attacks. Someone made a storage bucket public to share a file "for a day". A test server was left with remote desktop open to the whole internet. The original admin account, created when the company first signed up, still has no MFA and a password that three former staff knew.

The US National Security Agency put it plainly when it published its Top Ten Cloud Security Mitigation Strategies in March 2024: many cloud breaches come down to misconfigurations in the customer's own tenant. CISA co-authored several of those guidance sheets, and they are worth reading in full. This post is the short, practical version for a company that runs a few things on AWS, Azure or Google Cloud and does not have a security team.

That is where a HackRF with a PortaPack earns its place on the bench.

As a hypothetical example, a software firm in Colombo 03 runs an internal bootcamp. Week one is 2.4 GHz only on a locked lab AP. The mentor’s job is to keep the first success close enough that students do not equate wireless security with driver hell.

Wireless labs die in two boring ways: the wrong chipset, or the right chipset jammed against a metal laptop hinge. The zSecurity RTL8812AU adapter is ALFA Network LK’s zSecurity-branded dual-band USB 3.0 option for authorised Kali-style work — monitor mode, injection practice, and capture homework on networks you are allowed to touch.

Imagine this: a university NOC in Peradeniya stands up a 5 GHz-only lab SSID so students stop camping on the crowded 2.4 GHz classroom channel. Half the borrowed dongles are single-band. The session stalls. A dual-band RTL8812AU-class card with detachable antennas is the unglamorous fix that lets the mentor keep the timetable.
